critique.good: The Plan → List price → Billing terms run reads cleanly: identity column is uninterrupted, the bold $ amounts sit right beside their explanation, and at 170px the terms cell settles into 4–5 lines with no mid-word splits. Row heights 83–129 are the most even of the three.

critique.cause: 96+88+170 = 354px of the 359px budget is consumed by the three left columns, so cols 4–6 (87/84/100 = 271px) fall entirely outside the visible 360px; the 170px terms width is what sets the 4–5 line, 106–129px rows.

critique.good: The only design that gets the fourth column (Minimum seats) into the first scroll page, and it sits closest to the theoretical minimum table width (562px vs. 359 available), so the reader scrolls least. Zero mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Catastrophic vertical rhythm: rows range 60–199px, the tallest cell is 8 lines, and the table is 1082px tall — it stops reading as a grid of comparable rows and becomes a stack of paragraphs. 'Minimum seats' header wraps while its values are single digits, wasting a wrapped header on a 2-character column.
critique.cause: The 107px Billing terms column (86px of content) is narrower than the unbreakable word 'commitment' (86px), so every sentence is broken at ~86px into 6–8 short lines; that single width dictates every tall row.

critique.good: Cleanest type: no header wraps at all, terms at 160px holds 5 lines max, and the wider 130/110/130 attribute columns give the checklist strip breathing room.
critique.problems: Overflows the most (355px) while still showing only Plan/Price inside the box — so the extra 90px spent on seats/contract/support bought nothing visible or useful, since those values ('25', 'Annual', '24/7') are short. Tallest cell 5 lines, rows up to 129px.
critique.cause: Width was added to cols 4–6 (130/110/130), whose content one-lines are only 109/123/195px, instead of to col 3, whose 490px one-liner is the only real driver of row height; total 715px vs. r1A's 626px for the same 5-line worst cell.

critique.good: Cleanest left edge: Plan at 96 holds 'Education' on one line, and the Price pair sits adjacent with all seven headers on a single line. Row heights stay lowest of the three (max 3 lines, table 547px tall), so rows read as compact bands.
critique.problems: Still overflows by 375px, and the three attribute columns (seats/contract/support) are pushed entirely out of the 360px box — the reader sees plan, price and billing terms but never the checklist. It is also the most wasteful: billing terms gets 220px (text 199) for prose that reads fine at ~150, while cols 4–6 sit at 100/105/125 — near but below their one-line needs (109/123/195), so Support values still wrap for no gain.
critique.cause: Col 3 is over-allocated at 220 while cols 4–6 are given generous but insufficient widths; the sum is 735 because no column was compressed to its unbreakable minimum (87/84/100).

critique.good: Narrowest of the three (635) and it is the only one that shows a sliver of 'Minimum seats' inside the box, hinting at the attribute strip. Plan column again intact, no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Worst proportion: narrowest yet tallest (756px, 5-line cells, rows 106–129). Billing terms at 150 (text 129) shreds the prose into 4–5 short lines, and cols 4–6 at 95/95/110 are below even the unbreakable-word widths for 'Minimum seats' (66) and 'Support' (79) plus values, so those columns are both cramped and still off-screen. It buys no fit and pays in height.
critique.cause: Width was spread thin across all six columns: col 3 squeezed to 150 without shrinking cols 4–6 to their true minimums, so the 275px overflow remained while wrapping exploded.

critique.good: Best internal proportions: billing 170 (text 149) gives readable 4–5 line prose, and cols 4–6 at 109/123/150 match their one-line content widths so those headers and values stay on one line with no splits. Consistent rhythm across the attribute strip.
critique.problems: Widest table (737) with the largest overflow (377), and the entire attribute strip is off-screen, defeating the checklist role. Table is also 686 tall. Support at 150 is still short of its 195 one-line need, so some support values wrap anyway — paying width without getting the full benefit.
critique.cause: Cols 4–6 were given their full one-line widths (382px combined, more than the whole 360px box) on top of a 170px billing column; the six widths were never reconciled against a total budget.

understanding.purpose: A procurement/comparison reference: pick a plan (row) and read its price, how it is billed, seat minimums, contract and support terms. It is scanned vertically by plan and compared horizontally by attribute.
understanding.reading: Reader anchors on column 1 (Plan), reads the bold price, then the billing-terms sentence that explains it, then the three short constraint/attribute columns (seats, contract, support) as a quick checklist. So the eye moves plan → price pair → terms strip, and column 3's long prose is the one cell that must wrap.
groups: cols 2+3 (Price group): 'List price' is the number, 'Billing terms' its explanation — they must stay adjacent under the merged 'Price' header and be read as a pair
cols 4,5,6 (Minimum seats / Contract / Support): same role — short attribute values in a checklist strip; they should share a similar, compact rhythm even if their headers are narrower than one line
col 1 (Plan) stands alone as row identity and needs a clean, uninterrupted edge
keep_intact: Plan names (Education = 75px) — never split a row identifier
Currency amounts ($12, $45) and the price column header 'List price' (67px)
Short contract/support values and their header words if any scroll budget exists
may_wrap: Billing terms prose (490px one-line) — the natural flexible column; 2–6 lines are acceptable and absorb row-height growth
'Minimum seats', 'Contract', 'Support' headers into two lines if width forces it
Billing-terms header word 'Billing' only as a last resort

bad.why: Billing terms is squeezed to 107px, producing 8-line cells and a 1082px-tall table; the prose column becomes a narrow ribbon that is hard to scan, and the table still overflows.
Billing terms is only 128px, forcing 6-line cells and an 826px-tall table while still overflowing by 198px; it is both scroll-heavy and vertically bloated.

final.rationale: r3C is the best phone compromise: its first three columns (Plan, List price, Billing terms) total 366px, so the core pricing information is almost exactly one viewport wide while the secondary columns scroll. Giving Billing terms 210px keeps the longest cells to three lines and the table to 593px high without mid-word splits. The 60px List price column still holds $12/$45 intact and wraps its two-word header cleanly; the tight secondary columns are acceptable because they are secondary and wrap at word boundaries.

general: Allocate width by information role: prose columns need the most space; identifier and price columns need just enough to stay intact.
On phones, try to keep the primary reading path (row label plus key values) within one viewport; let secondary columns scroll.
A two-word header wrapping at a space is usually preferable to squeezing a prose column into 4–6 lines or splitting words.
Avoid designs that both overflow and remain very tall; that is the worst of both worlds.
specific: Billing terms is the only long-prose column and drives row height; 210px gives three lines, while 170px or less forces four to five and 107px forces eight.
Plan needs 96px and List price about 60px to keep 'Enterprise' and '$12' intact; the List price header can wrap cleanly at the space.
Minimum seats, Contract and Support can be 87/84/100px because their headers and data wrap at word boundaries and they are secondary.
r3C's core Plan + Price width is 366px, almost exactly the 360px viewport; r2A's core is 404px.

final.tradeoffs: r2A is 46px shorter and has only one wrapped header, but it is 97px wider and pushes the core price columns further off-screen; r3B is 35px narrower but 70px taller. The choice depends on whether horizontal scroll or vertical length costs the reader more.
final.uncertain: Whether the 60px List price column feels too tight in practice; whether Support's data needs more than 100px; whether a three-line Billing terms cell is acceptable or two lines are required. A designer could reasonably prefer r2A for its cleaner headers and shorter rows.

A.why: Billing terms is squeezed to ~110px so every cell wraps to 6–9 short lines, making rows enormously tall, and Contract and Support are still pushed off-screen — the worst of both worlds.

B.why: Nearly identical to A: 'List price' splits onto two lines, billing text fragments into many 2–3-word lines, rows are very tall, and the last two columns are cut off anyway.

C.why: Words stay intact and billing terms reads in 3–4 lines, giving compact rows and a visible sliver of Minimum seats, but the fourth column is truncated at the edge and the plan/price pairing is less crisp than in D/E.

D.why: Clean header hierarchy with 'List price' on one line and billing terms at a comfortable ~2–3 lines per row; rows read as units. Cost: only three columns are visible and some billing text runs past the right edge.

E.why: Compact, readable rows with no mid-word breaks, billing text fully visible at two lines, clear Plan/Price grouping; sacrifices Contract/Support and wraps the 'List price' header, but the visible part is well proportioned.

F.why: All six columns forced into 360px: every word is split mid-word ('Start er', 'Busi ness', 'Billin g term s'), columns are ~40px wide and the table becomes ~1500px tall — essentially unreadable.

reviewsOld.unsure: Whether horizontal scrolling is actually available in the reader; if hidden columns are heavily penalised, C (which reveals part of Minimum seats) might edge out D/E.

A.why: All six columns are crushed into the 360px box; plan names and headers split mid-word ('Start er', 'Billin g term s'), billing text becomes a vertical ribbon, and rows are enormously tall, destroying scanability.

B.why: Plan, List price, Billing terms and Minimum seats are legible with no mid-word breaks; the Price group stays coherent and the cut after Minimum seats is relatively clean, though Billing terms is narrow and Contract/Support are off-screen.

C.why: Very readable Plan/List/Billing terms with comfortable billing lines and compact rows, but it gives almost all remaining width to Billing terms and hides Minimum seats, Contract and Support, so key comparisons are missing from the viewport.

D.why: Billing terms is cramped and the next column is sliced mid-word at the edge ('Co', 'Mo', 'or', 'an'), creating broken text and a messy scroll boundary while Support remains unseen.

E.why: Billing terms is fairly readable and Minimum seats values peek in, but its header is cut ('Mini... seats') and Contract/Support are off-screen; the partial column weakens the header hierarchy.

F.why: Billing terms is oversized and runs past the viewport, cutting sentences mid-word at the right edge; only Plan/Price are fully readable and the other three columns are hidden.

reviewsOld.unsure: I am judging the visible 360px viewport; I cannot tell how cleanly the off-screen columns scroll or whether B/C/E were intended as fixed-width scroll layouts. B vs C is a tradeoff between showing more columns and giving Billing terms more width.
